title: Leader Election
subtitle: Preventing Split-Brain using consensus leases, heartbeats, monotonic epochs, and Fencing Tokens.
keyTakeaways: Leader election designates a single coordinator node to serialize state mutations and prevent split-brain execution across distributed workers.
A leader can become a Zombie Leader due to JVM garbage collection pauses or network stalls; it wakes up still believing it is the leader.
Fencing tokens (monotonically increasing generation numbers) are mandatory to protect downstream storage from zombie leader writes.

[ Leader 1 Wakes Up! ]                 |
- Still thinks it is leader!           |
- Attempts write with Token 34 ------->+---> REJECTED! Storage sees Token 34 < 35 (Corruption Prevented)

sections.heading: How Leader Election Operates in Consensus Stores
sections.body: In architectures requiring single-point coordination (such as Kafka partition leaders, database primaries, or job schedulers), nodes elect a leader using consensus systems like etcd, ZooKeeper, or Raft.
bullets: Ephemeral Leases: A candidate node acquires a key with a time-to-live lease (e.g., `PUT /election/leader node_1 LEASE=10s`). If the node holds the key, it is the recognized leader.

Heartbeat Keep-Alive: The leader continuously sends heartbeats to renew its lease before expiry. If the leader crashes, the lease expires, deleting the key and allowing other nodes to compete for leadership.

sections.heading: The Zombie Leader Problem and Fencing Tokens
sections.body: The most dangerous failure in leader election is the Zombie Leader. Consider Leader 1 holding an active lease. Leader 1 suddenly encounters a 30-second Stop-the-World garbage collection pause. While it is frozen, its 10-second lease expires in etcd. The remaining cluster nodes elect Leader 2, which claims leadership and begins writing to storage.
bullets: The Awakening Hazard: Leader 1's GC pause ends. Its code resumes execution at the next line, unaware that 30 seconds have elapsed and it was deposed. It sends a write to storage, corrupting data written by Leader 2.

Fencing Tokens: Storage must enforce fencing tokens. Whenever a leader is elected, it is issued a monotonically increasing epoch number (e.g., Token 35). Storage records the highest token it has observed. When Leader 1 sends a write with Token 34, storage rejects it because `34 < 35`.

tradeOffs.pros: Strict mutual exclusion; automated failover upon crash; provides monotonically increasing fencing revisions.
tradeOffs.cons: Introduces external consensus infrastructure dependency; misconfigured timeouts cause unnecessary leadership thrashing.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Distributed database primary election, cron job schedulers, and Kafka controller election.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero leader election overhead; no single-leader bottleneck or failover downtime.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires distributed quorum logic and conflict resolution across all writes; higher network complexity.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume telemetry ingestion, object storage, and peer-to-peer data replication.

interviewTip: Distinguish yourself by explaining Martin Kleppmann's fencing token defense: 'Leases alone cannot guarantee mutual exclusion because an operating system GC pause or network stall can cause a leader to wake up and execute a write after its lease expired. Storage must validate monotonically increasing fencing tokens to reject stale writes from zombie leaders.'
